blocks.text: A petrol car and a diesel truck both burn hydrocarbon fuel in a piston and cylinder, yet the truck typically converts 40% of fuel energy to work and the car about 30%. Part of the gap is the thermodynamic cycle: the diesel can safely compress air to 18 times its volume, while the petrol mixture would knock. The air-standard model lets us compute the ideal efficiencies and see why.

blocks.markdown: In the **air-standard** analysis the working fluid is a fixed mass of air treated as an ideal gas with constant specific heats ($k = c_p/c_v = 1.4$). Combustion is replaced by heat addition from an external source, exhaust by heat rejection, and all processes are internally reversible. The **compression ratio** is $r = V_{max}/V_{min} = V_1/V_2$, the ratio of cylinder volume at bottom dead centre to the volume at top dead centre.

blocks.title: Otto cycle (spark ignition)
blocks.text: 1-2 isentropic compression; 2-3 constant-volume heat addition (rapid combustion at TDC); 3-4 isentropic expansion; 4-1 constant-volume heat rejection (exhaust blowdown).

blocks.caption: Depends only on the compression ratio $r$ and $k$ (air-standard, $k = 1.4$).

blocks.title: Otto cycle efficiency
blocks.prompt: A spark-ignition engine has a compression ratio of 9.5. Find the ideal air-standard efficiency with $k = 1.4$.

steps.text: Identify the formula and the exponent $k - 1 = 0.4$.

blocks.answer: Efficiency = 59.4%. Real engines reach about 30 to 35% because of friction, heat loss, incomplete combustion and variable specific heats.

blocks.title: Diesel cycle (compression ignition)
blocks.text: 1-2 isentropic compression of air only; 2-3 constant-pressure heat addition as fuel is injected and burns; 3-4 isentropic expansion; 4-1 constant-volume heat rejection. The **cut-off ratio** $r_c = V_3/V_2$ measures how long the fuel burns at constant pressure.

blocks.caption: $r_c > 1$ (cut-off ratio). The bracket is always greater than 1, so at equal $r$ the Diesel efficiency is below the Otto efficiency; as $r_c \to 1$ the bracket tends to 1.

blocks.title: Diesel cycle efficiency, with a temperature check
blocks.prompt: A diesel engine has compression ratio 18 and cut-off ratio 2.0, inlet air at $T_1 = 300$ K. Use $k = 1.4$, $c_p = 1.005$, $c_v = 0.718$ kJ/(kg K). Find the efficiency and verify with temperatures.

steps.text: Temperature check: $T_2 = T_1 r^{k-1}$, $T_3 = r_c T_2$, $T_4 = T_3 (r_c/r)^{k-1}$.

blocks.answer: Efficiency = 63.2%, confirmed by the temperature calculation (63.2%).

blocks.caption: Ideal air-standard efficiencies, $k = 1.4$, equal compression ratio.

blocks.markdown: At the **same compression ratio**, the Otto cycle is more efficient than the Diesel cycle, and the Diesel efficiency falls as the cut-off ratio (the amount of fuel burnt per cycle, or load) increases. But the Otto compression ratio cannot be raised freely. The petrol-air mixture is compressed together, and at high $r$ the end-gas temperature and pressure cause spontaneous ignition ahead of the flame front, called **knock** or detonation, which damages the engine. A typical limit for petrol engines is about 10 to 12. A diesel engine compresses only air and injects fuel at the end of compression, so it can use $r$ of roughly 14 to 23, giving a higher efficiency in practice.

blocks.title: Equal r vs real r
blocks.text: At equal compression ratio, $\eta_{Otto} > \eta_{Diesel}$. At the compression ratios each engine can actually use, the Diesel is the more efficient. Both comparisons are valid; state which one you are making.

items: Otto efficiency is independent of the heat added; Diesel efficiency falls with a bigger cut-off ratio (higher load).
Higher $k$ (monatomic-like gas) raises the efficiency; real mixtures have lower $k$ (about 1.3).
Both cycles reject heat at constant volume.
Compression ratio is geometric: $r = V_1/V_2$, and is not the pressure ratio.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Use $k - 1 = 0.4$, not $k$, in the exponent. Do not confuse cut-off ratio $r_c = V_3/V_2$ with compression ratio. Do not use the Otto formula for a diesel simply because the compression ratio is given.

points: At equal $r$, Otto exceeds Diesel; as $r_c \to 1$ they coincide.
Knock limits spark-ignition $r$; diesel engines compress only air, so can use higher $r$.

questions.stem: For an ideal air-standard Otto cycle, the thermal efficiency depends on

options.text: the heat added per cycle and the peak temperature
the cut-off ratio and the compression ratio
the compression ratio and the specific heat ratio only
the engine speed and displacement

questions.correctOptionText: the compression ratio and the specific heat ratio only

distractorRationale.a: These do not appear in the Otto efficiency formula.
distractorRationale.b: The cut-off ratio is a Diesel parameter.
distractorRationale.d: These affect power, not ideal efficiency.

questions.explanation: The Otto efficiency is $1 - r^{1-k}$, which contains only the compression ratio $r$ and $k$. Engine speed and displacement affect power, not cycle efficiency.

questions.stem: Why is the compression ratio of a spark-ignition petrol engine limited to about 10 to 12?

options.text: The air-fuel mixture would auto-ignite (knock) if compressed to a higher pressure and temperature
The Otto efficiency formula gives a decreasing efficiency above that ratio
Pistons cannot move faster than the speed of sound
The air would become a liquid

questions.correctOptionText: The air-fuel mixture would auto-ignite (knock) if compressed to a higher pressure and temperature

distractorRationale.b: Efficiency in fact keeps increasing with $r$.
distractorRationale.c: This is unrelated to compression ratio.
distractorRationale.d: Air does not liquefy at these temperatures.

questions.explanation: In a petrol engine the fuel and air are compressed together, so at high $r$ the end-gas temperature rises above the ignition temperature before the flame arrives. The resulting knock can damage the engine, which sets the practical limit on $r$.

questions.stem: For the same compression ratio and the same $k$, which statement about the ideal Otto and Diesel cycles is correct?

options.text: The Diesel cycle is more efficient than the Otto cycle
They are equally efficient
It depends on the heat input for both
The Otto cycle is more efficient than the Diesel cycle

questions.correctOptionText: The Otto cycle is more efficient than the Diesel cycle

distractorRationale.c: Otto efficiency does not depend on heat input; Diesel depends on cut-off ratio but is always lower.

questions.explanation: The Diesel bracket $(r_c^k - 1)/[k(r_c - 1)]$ is greater than 1 for $r_c > 1$, so $\eta_{Diesel} < \eta_{Otto}$ at equal $r$. Diesel engines win in practice only because they can use a higher $r$.

questions.stem: A diesel engine runs at a fixed compression ratio. As the load (and so the cut-off ratio) increases, what happens to its ideal air-standard efficiency?

options.text: It increases
It decreases
It is unchanged
It first increases then decreases

distractorRationale.a: The bracket in the Diesel formula grows with $r_c$, lowering efficiency.

questions.explanation: The factor $(r_c^k - 1)/[k(r_c - 1)]$ increases from 1 as $r_c$ rises. Since it is subtracted from 1, efficiency falls with load, which is why part-load diesels remain efficient.

questions.stem: A student uses $k = 1.3$ instead of 1.4 (to approximate hot combustion gases) in the Otto efficiency formula at the same compression ratio. What is the effect?

options.text: The calculated efficiency is higher
The calculated efficiency is unchanged
The calculated efficiency is lower
The efficiency becomes independent of $r$

distractorRationale.a: $r^{1-k}$ is larger for smaller $k$, so $\eta$ is smaller.

questions.explanation: Lowering $k$ makes $1-k$ less negative, so $r^{1-k}$ is larger and $\eta = 1 - r^{1-k}$ is lower. This is one reason that real engines have lower efficiency than cold air-standard predictions.

questions.stem: An ideal Otto engine has a compression ratio of 8.5. Taking $k = 1.4$, calculate its thermal efficiency as a percentage.
A diesel engine has a compression ratio of 16 and a cut-off ratio of 2.2. Taking $k = 1.4$, calculate the ideal air-standard efficiency as a percentage.
What compression ratio would an ideal air-standard Otto cycle need to have a thermal efficiency of 55%? Take $k = 1.4$ and give the compression ratio (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: Set $0.55 = 1 - r^{-0.4}$, so $r^{-0.4} = 0.45$ and $r = 0.45^{-2.5} = 7.362$. The result is quoted in dimensionless and is of a physically reasonable magnitude.

questions.stem: Compare the efficiency of an Otto and a Diesel cycle at equal compression ratio, and explain why real diesel engines are nevertheless usually more efficient than real petrol engines. Refer to the factor that limits the compression ratio of petrol engines.
markingGuide: At equal $r$, $\eta_{Otto} > \eta_{Diesel}$ because heat is added at constant volume in Otto (more efficient heat addition at high temperature and smaller volume)
The bracket factor in the Diesel formula is above 1 for $r_c > 1$
Petrol engines compress a fuel-air mixture and are limited by knock to $r \approx 10$ to 12
Diesel engines compress air alone, so $r \approx 14$ to 23 is possible
Higher $r$ outweighs the Diesel penalty, so practical Diesel engines are more efficient
Notes that Diesel efficiency falls with load (cut-off), but part-load diesel efficiency stays good due to unthrottled operation
questions.explanation: At equal $r$ the Otto cycle wins. But since petrol engines are knock-limited, a Diesel can use a much higher compression ratio and so reaches a higher efficiency in practice.

questions.stem: An Otto engine with $r = 10$ is compared with a Diesel engine with $r = 20$ and cut-off ratio 2.0, both with $k = 1.4$. Calculate both ideal efficiencies, state which is higher and explain what this comparison does and does not show about the two cycles.
markingGuide: States that the Diesel engine is higher here (64.7% vs 60.2%) because its compression ratio is double
Notes that at equal compression ratio, e.g. $r = 20$, Otto would be 69.8% and so higher still
The comparison shows that compression ratio can outweigh the cycle type: a high-$r$ Diesel beats a lower-$r$ Otto
It does not account for the knock limit that prevents Otto engines from using $r = 20$, or for real losses such as pumping and heat transfer
Concludes that the practical limits on $r$ decide the winner
questions.explanation: With the stated values the ideal Otto efficiency is 60.2% and the Diesel 64.7%. The Diesel is higher because $r$ is twice as large, even though at equal $r$ the Otto cycle would win; the knock limit prevents Otto engines from using such high $r$.
